options.why: `String.prototype.repeat` takes a count, so `times` is a number, and the return type is inferred as `string`. Every value is checked.
This compiles, but `any` switches checking off. `banner(5, 'x')` would compile and crash at runtime, which defeats the point of the task.
`repeat` expects a number, so passing a string `times` is a compile error (TS2345).
Under `strict`, the unannotated `name` is an implicit `any` and is reported (TS7006).

explanation: Typing a small JavaScript function is the most common TypeScript warm-up. Read how each parameter is used (`repeat` needs a number), annotate the parameters, and let the return type be inferred or write it out. Interviewers are checking that you reach for precise types instead of `any`, and that you know `strict` turns on `noImplicitAny`.

options.why: Every property is `unknown`, so `i.price * i.qty` fails until you narrow each value (TS18046).
It compiles, but every element is still `any`, and so is the return value. The `any` has only moved.
`unknown` is safe but unusable here: you can't call `reduce` on it without narrowing first (TS18046).
Each element now has a known `price` and `qty`, so `reduce` infers `sum` as `number` and the result is `number`.

explanation: Replacing `any` means describing the shape you actually use. Here that is an array of objects with numeric `price` and `qty`. `object` and `unknown` are too vague to use without extra checks, and `Array<any>` hides the same problem. Interviewers treat loose `any` as a negative signal, so a precise type is the expected fix.

options.text: `function toggle(todos: Todo[], id: number): readonly Todo[]`
options.why: Only the returned array is read-only. The input is a plain `Todo[]`, so the function can still mutate it.
It compiles, but `any[]` allows anything, including mutation and wrong element shapes.

options.text: `function toggle(todos: readonly Todo[], id: number): Todo[]`
options.why: A `readonly Todo[]` has no `push`, `sort` or index assignment, so accidental mutation is a compile error. `map` still returns a new `Todo[]`.
This makes each todo's properties read-only, but the array itself is mutable. `todos.push(...)` and `todos.sort()` still compile.

explanation: `readonly T[]` (or `ReadonlyArray<T>`) removes the mutating methods from the array type, so the compiler enforces the immutable-update style. `Readonly<Todo>[]` protects the elements, not the array. Annotating the return type as read-only does nothing for the input. This exercise checks that you can type a parameter and also express an intent such as "don't mutate" in the type.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Object Types (The ReadonlyArray Type)

options.why: The two operators are swapped here.
`||` falls back on any falsy value (`0`, `''`), while `??` falls back only on `null` or `undefined`.
That would mean `||` keeps falsy values. It doesn't: `0 || 50` is `50`.
That treats `??` like `||`. `0` and `''` are not nullish, so `??` keeps them.

explanation: `a || b` returns `b` whenever `a` is falsy, which includes `0`, `''`, `false` and `NaN`. `a ?? b` returns `b` only when `a` is `null` or `undefined`. For settings where `0` or an empty string is a real value, `??` is the right default operator. This is the classic follow-up interviewers ask after "what is nullish coalescing?".

options.why: Each `?.` stops and yields `undefined` when the value to its left is `null` or `undefined`, so the type gains `| undefined`. Here `address` is missing.
TypeScript adds `undefined` to the type of an optional chain, because the chain can stop early.
Optional chaining exists to avoid that error. `user.address.city` without `?.` would throw, and would not compile under `strict`.
A short-circuited optional chain produces `undefined`, never `null`.

explanation: `?.` reads a property only if the value on its left is not `null` or `undefined`. Otherwise the whole chain evaluates to `undefined`. TypeScript models this by adding `undefined` to the result type, so you still have to handle the missing case, often with `?? "unknown"`. Writing `user.address.city` here is a strict-mode error ("'user.address' is possibly 'undefined'").

options.why: `?.` only guards against `opts` being nullish. The `||` still replaces `0` with `0.1`.
`!` is a compile-time assertion with no runtime effect. The `||` behaves exactly as before.
Callers would have to pass a value, but `0 || 0.1` would still give `0.1`. The operator is the bug.
`??` uses `0.1` only when `discount` is missing (`undefined`) or `null`, so an explicit `0` is kept.

explanation: `||` treats every falsy value, including `0`, as missing. `??` treats only `null` and `undefined` as missing, which is what an optional numeric option needs. With `??`, `finalPrice(100, { discount: 0 })` returns `100`, and `finalPrice(100, {})` still applies the default and returns `90`.

stem: An interviewer asks: "What's the difference between `readonly` and `const`?" Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: `readonly` applies to a property (or an array or tuple type) and stops writes through that type
options.why: `readonly` is a modifier on properties, index signatures and array types, not on variables.

options.text: `readonly` is also enforced at runtime, so writing to the property throws in strict mode
options.why: `readonly` is erased from the JavaScript output. Only `Object.freeze` or a getter-only property stops writes at runtime.

options.text: `const` makes the whole object deeply immutable
options.why: `const` only protects the binding. Nested and top-level properties can still be changed.

options.text: You can write `readonly x = 5;` at the top level of a module instead of `const x = 5;`
options.why: `readonly` is not a variable declaration keyword. It is only valid on class properties, interface or type members, and array or tuple types.

options.text: `const` applies to a variable binding: the variable can't be reassigned, but the object it points to can still change
options.why: `const cfg = { a: 1 }; cfg.a = 2;` is allowed. Only `cfg = ...` is rejected.

explanation: A short way to say it: use `const` for variables and `readonly` for properties. `const` stops reassignment of the binding, and `readonly` stops writes to a property through a particular type. Neither makes values deeply immutable, and `readonly` exists only at compile time. For literal values, `as const` combines the two ideas by making every property `readonly` and keeping literal types.

options.why: `q` is a `let`, so it can point to a new `Point`. `readonly` limits writes to `x`, not replacing the whole object.
`limit` is a `const` binding and can't be reassigned (TS2588).
Spreading creates a new, ordinary `number[]`, so `push` is allowed on the copy.
`const` protects the `config` binding, not its properties, so changing `retries` is allowed.
`x` is `readonly` on `Point`, so assigning to it is TS2540.

explanation: `const` and `readonly` protect different things. `const` locks a variable binding, and `readonly` locks a property through a type. A `let` holding a `readonly` type can still be reassigned, and a `const` object can still have its properties changed. Copying a read-only array with spread gives you a normal mutable array.

options.why: Members of a `const enum` are inlined at each use, and the enum declaration is removed from the output.

options.text: A `Direction` object with a reverse mapping, and `const d = Direction.Down;`
options.why: That is the output for a regular `enum`. A `const enum` produces no runtime object.

options.text: `const Direction = Object.freeze({ Up: 1, Down: 2 });` and `const d = Direction.Down;`
options.why: TypeScript never emits `Object.freeze` for enums.

options.text: Nothing at all, because `const enum` values exist only at compile time
options.why: The declaration disappears, but `d` still needs its value, so `2` is inlined.

explanation: A regular enum compiles to an object (with a reverse mapping for numeric members), so you can iterate over it or look up `Direction[2]`. A `const enum` is inlined at every use and leaves no object behind, which makes the output smaller but means no runtime lookup. Because single-file transpilers such as Babel, esbuild and SWC can't see another file's enum values, `const enum` is restricted under `isolatedModules`. Many teams now prefer union types or `as const` objects instead.

stem: "Interface or abstract class: what's the difference?" Which three statements belong in a good answer? (Choose three.)

options.text: An interface can declare `private` members that implementing classes must also keep private
options.why: Interfaces describe the public shape only. Access modifiers are not allowed on interface members.

options.text: An abstract class can be instantiated with `new` once all of its abstract members have bodies
options.why: A class marked `abstract` can never be instantiated directly, whatever its members look like (TS2511).

options.text: Only interfaces can be used as the type of a variable or parameter
options.why: A class name, abstract or not, is also usable as a type.

options.text: An abstract class can contain a constructor, fields and implemented methods; an interface only describes a shape
options.why: Abstract classes often hold shared code. Interfaces have no implementation at all.

options.text: An abstract class exists at runtime, so `instanceof` works with it; an interface is erased
options.why: The abstract class is emitted as a normal JavaScript class. The interface leaves nothing in the output.

options.text: A class can implement several interfaces but can extend only one class, abstract or not
options.why: JavaScript has single inheritance; `implements` can list many interfaces.

explanation: Use an interface for a pure contract that many unrelated classes or plain objects can satisfy. Use an abstract class when subclasses should share real code or state and you want a runtime base you can check with `instanceof`. The interviewer wants the runtime difference (erased vs emitted), the implementation difference, and single vs multiple inheritance.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Classes (abstract Classes and Members)

stem: You are adding payment providers (Razorpay, Stripe, PayPal). Each one has its own `charge()` call, but all of them must share the same retry-with-backoff and logging code. Plain mock objects should not count as providers. Which design fits best?

options.text: An interface with an optional `chargeWithRetry?()` method that providers may implement
options.why: Interfaces can't carry a default implementation, and making it optional means callers must check whether it exists.

options.text: A union type `Razorpay | Stripe | PayPal` with a `switch` in every caller
options.why: This spreads the shared logic across callers and has to change every time a provider is added.

options.text: An abstract class `PaymentProvider` with an `abstract charge()` and a concrete `chargeWithRetry()` that calls it
options.why: The shared retry and logging logic lives once in the base class, and each provider only supplies `charge()`. A plain object can't extend the class, so the requirement holds at both compile time and runtime (`instanceof`).

options.text: An interface `PaymentProvider { charge(): Promise<void> }` that each provider implements
options.why: An interface can't hold the retry code, so each provider would copy it. Any object with a `charge` method would also satisfy it.

explanation: This is the template-method pattern. The abstract base class implements the common algorithm and leaves the varying step abstract. Interfaces are the better tool when you only need a contract, for example `Chargeable`, and possibly many implementations with nothing to share. Interviewers ask for a scenario like this to see whether you can justify the choice, not just list differences.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Classes (abstract Classes and Members)

options.why: `Shape` is an interface, so it only exists as a type: "'Shape' only refers to a type, but is being used as a value here" (TS2693).
An abstract class can't be instantiated directly (TS2511).
Any object with a matching `area` method satisfies an interface. No class is needed.

options.text: None of the four lines compile, because `Square` both extends and implements
options.why: A class can extend one class and implement interfaces at the same time.
`Base` is a real class at runtime, so `instanceof Base` works and narrows `x` to `Base`.

explanation: The runtime difference is the one candidates miss. An abstract class is emitted as JavaScript, so it works with `instanceof`, but it can't be created with `new`. An interface is erased, so you can't use it in `instanceof`. To check an interface at runtime you write a type guard instead (for example `"area" in x`).
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Classes (abstract Classes and Members)

stem: "How are TypeScript classes different from plain ES6 classes?" Which three of these class features exist only in TypeScript? (Choose three.)

options.text: Parameter properties, as in `constructor(private name: string) {}`
options.why: TypeScript expands this into a field plus `this.name = name`. Plain JavaScript has no such shorthand.
`abstract` is a TypeScript keyword. JavaScript has no way to forbid `new` on a class at the language level.
These are compile-time checks that are erased from the output.
`#` private fields are standard JavaScript (ES2022) and are enforced at runtime.
Static blocks are standard JavaScript (ES2022).
Accessors have been part of JavaScript classes since ES2015.

explanation: TypeScript classes are JavaScript classes plus a type layer: access modifiers (`public`, `private`, `protected`), `readonly`, `abstract`, `implements`, parameter properties and typed fields. Most of this is removed when compiling. A strong answer also mentions that `private` is compile-time only while `#private` is real runtime privacy.

options.text: Nothing; TypeScript infers the fields `x` and `y` from the assignments in the constructor
options.why: That inference happens only in JavaScript files checked by TypeScript, not in `.ts` files.

options.text: An error saying the constructor needs a return type annotation
options.why: Constructors never take a return type annotation.

options.text: An error saying that `x` and `y` must be marked `public`
options.why: Members are public by default. The problem is that they aren't declared at all.

options.text: "Property 'x' does not exist on type 'Point'" (and the same for `y`), because fields must be declared
options.why: In TypeScript a class's instance shape comes from its declarations. Assigning to an undeclared `this.x` is an error (TS2339).

explanation: In ES6 you can create instance properties just by assigning to `this`. TypeScript wants them declared, either as fields (`x: number;`) or as parameter properties (`constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {}`). This is one of the first things people meet when moving a JavaScript class to TypeScript.

options.text: A `typeof age === "number"` check in the constructor
options.why: TypeScript never emits runtime type checks for annotations.

options.text: Assignments `this.name = name;` and `this.age = age;` inside the constructor
options.why: Parameter properties are compiled into ordinary assignments in the constructor.
The class itself is real JavaScript and is emitted.
Access modifiers are erased. At runtime `age` is a normal public property.
`implements` is a compile-time check only, and the `Named` interface is erased.

explanation: TypeScript class syntax is mostly erased: interfaces, `implements`, access modifiers and type annotations all disappear. What remains is the JavaScript class, and parameter properties turn into real assignments. That's why `private` doesn't stop `(user as any).age` at runtime, and why `#age` is the choice when you need runtime privacy.

stem: You want `greet` to take an object with a string `name` and a number `age`. Which declaration compiles under `strict` and types both properties?

options.text: `function greet(name: string, age: number) { ... }` called as `greet({ name, age })`
options.why: That signature takes two separate arguments, so passing one object is a compile error ("Expected 2 arguments, but got 1").

options.text: `function greet({ name, age }: { name: string; age: number }) { ... }`
options.why: The type annotation goes after the whole destructuring pattern, as a type for the single object parameter.
Inside a destructuring pattern, `name: string` means "rename `name` to a variable called `string`". Both new variables are implicit `any` under `strict` (TS7031).
This is a syntax error: a destructuring pattern uses commas and has no type positions.

explanation: When you destructure a parameter, the type describes the whole object and follows the pattern: `({ a, b }: { a: string; b: number })`. A named type keeps it readable: `({ name, age }: Person)`. The `{ name: string }` form is a common trap, because the colon inside a pattern renames the property instead of typing it.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: More on Functions (Parameter Destructuring)

stem: A logger takes a level and then any number of message strings, as in `log("warn", "disk", "almost full")`. Which declaration compiles?

options.why: A rest parameter collects the remaining arguments into an array, so its type is an array type, and it comes last.
A rest parameter must have an array (or tuple) type (TS2370).
A rest parameter must be the last parameter (TS1014).
This is not valid syntax. The `...` belongs before the parameter name.

explanation: Rest parameters are written `...name: T[]` (or a tuple type) and must come last. Inside the function, `messages` is a normal `string[]`. Default values go on the parameter itself, as in `level = "info"`, and TypeScript infers `string` from the default.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: More on Functions (Rest Parameters)

options.why: An arrow function doesn't get the instance as `this`; it captures the outer `this`. Under `strict` this is a compile error ("'this' implicitly has type 'any'").
This compiles, but `target(...args)` drops `this`. `new Cart().count()` throws "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'items')".
This is the legacy `experimentalDecorators` signature. Standard decorators receive two arguments, so TypeScript reports TS1241.
It returns a regular function, so `this` is the instance at call time, and `target.call(this, ...args)` forwards both. The generics keep the method's types.

explanation: A TypeScript 5 method decorator receives the original method and a context object, and it can return a replacement function. The replacement must be a regular `function` so it receives the instance as `this`, and it must forward `this` with `call` or `apply`. The three-argument `(target, key, descriptor)` form is the older experimental API that Angular and NestJS still use, and it needs `experimentalDecorators`. Interviewers like to ask which of the two you are using.

options.why: The decorator runs as part of the class declaration, which comes before `console.log("start")`.

options.text: `start`, `constructed`, `constructed`; class decorators only take effect with `experimentalDecorators`
options.why: Standard decorators work in TypeScript 5 without any flag.
A class decorator runs once, when the class is defined, before any of the following code runs. Creating instances doesn't run it again.
Decorators are not called on each `new`. They run once at class definition.

explanation: Decorators are functions that run when the class is defined. A class decorator receives the class itself and a context with `kind: "class"` and the class `name`. It can return a replacement class. Frameworks use this moment to register metadata: Angular's `@Component` and NestJS's `@Injectable` record information about the class so the framework can create it later.

options.why: A `using` resource stays alive until the end of the enclosing block.
Resources are disposed when the block ends, in reverse order of declaration, like a stack.
Disposal is last-in, first-out, so `b` is closed before `a`.
Disposal happens when `run`'s block exits, not later after other code.

explanation: A `using` declaration (explicit resource management) calls the value's `[Symbol.dispose]()` method automatically when the enclosing block exits. Several resources are disposed in reverse order, so later resources that may depend on earlier ones are cleaned up first. It replaces hand-written `try`/`finally` cleanup for file handles, locks and connections. The async form is `await using` with `[Symbol.asyncDispose]()`.
reference: TypeScript 5.2 release notes: using Declarations and Explicit Resource Management

options.why: Disposal runs as the `try` block exits, even when it exits by throwing, and before the `catch` runs.
`l` is scoped to the `try` block, so it is disposed as soon as that block exits, before the handler runs.
Cleanup on exceptions is the main reason `using` exists; it behaves like a `finally`.

options.text: It doesn't compile: an object literal can't be used with `using`
options.why: Any object with a `[Symbol.dispose]()` method is accepted. Only values without it (other than `null` or `undefined`) are rejected (TS2850).

explanation: `using` works like an automatic `finally`. When the block exits, whether normally, by `return` or by `throw`, the resource's `[Symbol.dispose]()` runs, and then the exception continues to the `catch`. If disposal itself throws while an error is already in flight, both errors are combined in a `SuppressedError`. The interviewer is checking that you understand it as guaranteed cleanup, not just new syntax.
reference: TypeScript 5.2 release notes: using Declarations and Explicit Resource Management

options.text: Write `if (pet instanceof Cat)` instead, because `instanceof` works with type aliases
options.why: `Cat` is a type alias and is erased. `instanceof` needs a runtime constructor (TS2693).
Both are objects, so this check is always true and narrows nothing; `pet.meow()` is still an error.
The assertion compiles, but a `Dog` would crash at runtime because it has no `meow`.

options.text: Both are `"object"` to `typeof`; check `if ("meow" in pet)` instead
options.why: The `in` operator checks a property at runtime, and TypeScript narrows `pet` to `Cat` in that branch and `Dog` after it.

explanation: `typeof` only returns JavaScript's built-in categories (`"string"`, `"number"`, `"object"`, `"function"` and so on). Type names don't exist at runtime, which is why TypeScript reports that comparing with `"Cat"` has no overlap. To tell object shapes apart, use the `in` operator, a discriminant property such as `kind: "cat"`, `instanceof` with real classes, or a custom type guard.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Narrowing (The in operator narrowing)

stem: Interview task: write a generic `Stack<T>` with `push` and `pop`. Which version compiles under `strict` and keeps the element type?

options.why: `T` is declared only on `push`, so the field can't see it ("Cannot find name 'T'"). A class-wide type parameter belongs after the class name.
It compiles, but every popped value is `any`, so `const s: string = stack.pop()` compiles even after pushing numbers.
`T` is declared on the class, so every member shares it. `pop` honestly returns `T | undefined`, because the stack may be empty.
`Array.prototype.pop` returns `T | undefined`, so under `strict` this is TS2322: 'T | undefined' is not assignable to 'T'.

explanation: A generic class declares its type parameter after the class name, and every field and method uses the same `T`. The instance type is fixed when you write `new Stack<number>()` or when TypeScript infers it. Interviewers also look for an honest `pop()`/`peek()` return type of `T | undefined`, rather than hiding the empty case.

options.text: No errors; the stack infers `T` from the values pushed
options.why: Inference happens only from constructor arguments, and here `T` was given explicitly as `number`.

options.text: Errors on both line A and line B
options.why: With `T` fixed to `number`, `push` only accepts numbers, and `peek()` may return `undefined`, which a plain `number` can't hold.

options.text: An error only on line A
options.why: Line B is also an error: `top` has type `number | undefined`, and `undefined` is not assignable to `number` under `strict`.

options.text: An error only on line B; `push` widens `T` to `string | number`
options.why: An explicit type argument fixes `T` when the instance is created. Later calls can't widen it.

explanation: Once you write `new Stack<number>()`, `T` is `number` for that instance, so `push("2")` fails with TS2345. The stack can be empty, so `peek()` returns `number | undefined`, and you need a check (`if (top !== undefined)`) or a default (`?? 0`) before using it as a `number`. This is the follow-up question that comes after "write a generic stack".

stem: Write a generic `ApiResponse<T>` type: a response holds either the data (`T`) or an error message, never both and never neither. Which declaration enforces that?

options.text: `type ApiResponse<T> = { success: true; data: T } | { success: false; error: string };`
options.why: A discriminated union: the literal `success` field picks the variant, and each variant has exactly the fields it needs.
Both `{}` and `{ data, error }` are valid values of this type, so it allows neither or both.

options.text: `type ApiResponse<T> = { success: boolean; data: T | null; error: string | null };`
options.why: Nothing ties `success` to which field is set, so `{ success: true, data: null, error: "x" }` is valid.
It isn't generic, and `any` throws away the data type.

explanation: Model the two outcomes as separate object types joined by a union, with a literal discriminant (`success`, `ok` or `status`). Callers must check the discriminant before reading `data`, and TypeScript narrows to the right variant. Optional fields look simpler but allow invalid states. The interviewer wants to see you make invalid states impossible to represent.

options.why: `!` removes `null` and `undefined`; it doesn't add a missing property. This is still TS2339.
It compiles, but it crashes when the request failed, because `data` is then `undefined`.
This only changes `T`. The union still has a variant without `data`, so the property access still fails.

options.text: Check `if (res.success)` first and read `res.data.name` inside that branch
options.why: Checking the discriminant narrows `res` to the success variant, where `data: User` exists.

explanation: With a discriminated union, you can only read the fields common to every variant (here just `success`) until you narrow. Checking `res.success` is the narrowing step, and the `else` branch gets `res.error`. This is the point of the wrapper: the compiler won't let anyone use `data` without handling the error case.

stem:
You add a helper that returns the data or throws:

```ts
type ApiResponse<T> = { success: true; data: T } | { success: false; error: string };
```

Which implementation compiles under `strict`?

options.text: `function unwrap<T>(r: ApiResponse<T>): T { return r.success ? r.data : null; }`
options.why: `null` is not assignable to `T` (TS2322). The return type would have to be `T | null`.

options.text: `function unwrap<T>(r: ApiResponse<T>): T { if (!r.success) { console.error(r.error); } return r.data; }`
options.why: Logging doesn't leave the function, so after the `if` `r` can still be either variant, and `r.data` is TS2339.

options.text: `function unwrap<T>(r: ApiResponse<T>): T { if (r.success) return r.data; throw new Error(r.error); }`
options.why: Inside the `if`, `r` is the success variant; after it, TypeScript knows `r` is the failure variant, so `r.error` is a string.
`data` doesn't exist on the failure variant, so reading it without narrowing is TS2339.

explanation: Narrowing follows control flow. Only a branch that returns or throws removes the failure variant from what comes after it. A `T` return type means every path must produce a `T` or throw. Writing `unwrap` this way gives callers a plain `T` and turns API errors into exceptions in one checked place.

options.why: `Awaited<Promise<number>>` is just `number`, so this is the same TS1064 error.
An `async` function always returns a promise, so its declared return type must be `Promise<T>` of the value it returns.
TS1064: the return type of an async function must be the global `Promise<T>` type.
Returning `42` from a function declared to resolve to `void` is TS2322.

explanation: `async` wraps whatever you `return` in a promise, so `getCount()` is inferred as `Promise<number>` and an explicit annotation must say the same. Inside the function you write `return 42`, not `return Promise.resolve(42)`. Errors are not part of the type: a rejected promise has no type parameter for its error, and `catch (e)` gives `e: unknown` under `strict`.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: More on Functions (Return type of async functions)

stem: Write the type for your own `all` function so that `await all([userPromise, 42, namePromise])` has type `[User, number, string]`. `userPromise` is a `Promise<User>` and `namePromise` is a `Promise<string>`. Which signature does it?

options.text: `declare function all<T extends readonly unknown[]>(values: [...T]): Promise<{ -readonly [K in keyof T]: Awaited<T[K]> }>;`
options.why: `[...T]` makes TypeScript infer a tuple, not an array. Mapping over a tuple keeps each position, and `Awaited` unwraps each one.

options.text: `declare function all<T extends unknown[]>(values: T): Promise<{ [K in keyof T]: Awaited<T[K]> }>;`
options.why: Without `[...T]`, the array literal is inferred as `(number | Promise<User> | Promise<string>)[]`, so the result is `(string | number | User)[]`.
One `T` must fit every element, so mixing `Promise<User>` and `Promise<string>` is a compile error, and the plain `42` isn't a promise.

options.text: `declare function all<T extends readonly unknown[]>(values: T): Promise<Awaited<T[number]>[]>;`
options.why: `T[number]` merges all elements into one union, giving `(string | number | User)[]` and losing positions.

explanation: Two ideas are needed. First, a variadic tuple hint (`[...T]`) so the argument is inferred as a tuple. Second, a mapped type over that tuple, which maps each element separately and keeps the tuple shape, with `Awaited` to unwrap promises and pass plain values through. This is essentially how the built-in `Promise.all` is declared. Interviewers use it to check that you understand tuple inference, not just generics.
reference: TypeScript 4.0 release notes: Variadic Tuple Types

You need a type for `curry` that turns `(n: number, unit: string, upper: boolean) => string` into `(arg: number) => (arg: string) => (arg: boolean) => string`.

```ts
declare function curry<A extends unknown[], R>(fn: (...args: A) => R): Curried<A, R>;
```

Which definition of `Curried` does that?

options.text:
```ts
type Curried<A extends unknown[], R> =
  A extends [infer F, ...infer Rest]
    ? (arg: F) => Curried<Rest, R>
    : never;
```
options.why: With no parameters left, the recursion hits `never` instead of `R`, so `curry(fmt)(5)("kg")(true)` has type `never`.

options.text:
```ts
type Curried<A extends unknown[], R> =
  A extends [unknown, ...infer Rest]
    ? (arg: A[number]) => (Rest extends [] ? R : Curried<Rest, R>)
    : R;
```
options.why: `A[number]` is a union of all remaining parameter types, so the first call accepts `"5"` or `true` as well as a number. Positions are lost.
This only handles the first argument and claims that one call returns the final result.

options.text:
```ts
type Curried<A extends unknown[], R> =
  A extends [infer F, ...infer Rest]
    ? (arg: F) => (Rest extends [] ? R : Curried<Rest, R>)
    : R;
```
options.why: It peels off the first parameter, returns a one-argument function for it, and recurses on the rest. When nothing is left, the last function returns `R`.

explanation: Typed currying needs a recursive conditional type over the parameter tuple: `infer` the head, produce `(arg: Head) => ...`, and recurse on the tail until it is empty, then return `R`. Variants that also allow several arguments per call use the same recursion with variadic tuples. Getting the base case right (`R`, not `never`) is the detail interviewers watch for.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Conditional Types (Inferring Within Conditional Types)

options.why: That is the type of `curry(fmt)` itself, before the first call.
Two more arguments are still needed before the original function runs.
`curry(fmt)` is `(arg: number) => (arg: string) => (arg: boolean) => string`, and calling it once with `5` removes the first layer.
This `Curried` type returns one-argument functions at every step; it never groups the remaining parameters.

explanation: Each call to a curried function removes one parameter from the front of the tuple. Reading recursive types one layer at a time like this is how interviewers check that you understand the type you wrote, rather than having memorised it. TypeScript also checks each step: `curry(fmt)("5")` is an error because the first parameter is `number`.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Conditional Types (Inferring Within Conditional Types)
